newsitem.title: CHINA: China Resources denies allegations on Lippo ties.
newsitem.headline: China Resources denies allegations on Lippo ties.

text.p: Chinese conglomerate China Resources on Thursday launched a campaign to defend its name and threatened legal action over criticism made in a U.S. congressional hearing into foreign political funding.
The state-owned conglomerate's Hong Kong-based arm, China Resources (Holdings) Co Ltd, said it was the victim of "irresponsible, malicious and slanderous attacks on the company's reputation".

One of China's most powerful companies in this former British colony, China Resources took out a half-page advertisement in Hong Kong newspapers to deny allegations about its business and a relationship with Indonesia's Lippo Group.

"It has come to our attention that a witness testifying before the United States Senate Committee investigating campaign financing has made allegations about our business activities and our relationship with the Lippo Group," the advert said.
"Such allegations are entirely false and groundless. The company's business and relationships are entered into on a purely commercial basis," it said.

"The company has retained U.S. legal counsel to investigate its legal options regarding these irresponsible, malicious and slanderous attacks on the company's reputation. We will take all appropriate legal actions to clear our good name," it said.
China Resources officials contacted by Reuters declined to discuss the issue further.

At a Senate hearing last week, committee chairman Senator Fred Thompson said China Resources was principal partner in China of the Indonesian Lippo Group and that there were indications of a plot by China to influence U.S. elections.

On Tuesday this week, business consultant Thomas Hampson told the committee Lippo was increasing its ties with China, and claimed that China Resources, its main Chinese partner, was "an agent of espionage", the Congressional Report said.

The committee also heard on Tuesday that political fundraiser John Huang funnelled a US$50,000 contribution from Lippo Group in 1992 to the Democratic National Committee, and received a severance package of close to US$500,000 when he left Lippo Bank of Los Angeles to join the U.S. Commerce Department.

On Wednesday it heard that Huang received secret briefings about China and visited the Chinese embassy as a U.S. Commerce Department official even though his superior had walled him off from China policy.
China Resources, which has had a presence in Hong Kong for five decades, is under the direct control of communist-ruled China's Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation.
It engages in trading, property development, transport and warehousing, retailing, infrastructure, telecommunications and other business.
Its locally-listed trading conglomerate China Resources Enterprise Ltd was on Wednesday named a constituent stock for the blue-chip Hang Seng Index.
China Resources (Holdings) also indirectly controls food processor and distributor Ng Fung Hong Ltd.

On Tuesday the U.S. committee also made public a document that purportedly showed China-born Briton Eric Hotung of Hong Kong promised a US$100,000 contribution to the U.S. Democrats in 1995 in exchange for a meeting with Clinton's national security aides to seek a "higher profile for Taiwan on the world stage".
Hotung's spokesman told Reuters he was not in Hong Kong and added: "He said, 'At the right time you will get a statement'."
